intro.x: Chapters 1–5 worked with $\R^n$ and matrices. But the rules that made the computations work, namely that vectors can be added and scaled, are shared by many other objects: polynomials, continuous functions, sequences, matrices themselves, solutions of linear differential equations. A vector space is the abstract setting that captures exactly those rules. Working abstractly is not a luxury: it lets one proof cover all these examples at once, and it is the language in which the theory of Chapters 7–17 is stated.

blocks.x: A vector space over $\R$ is a set $V$ with two operations, addition $V\times V\to V$ and scalar multiplication $\R\times V\to V$, such that for all $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in V$ and $a,b\in\R$:
$\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}$;
$(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w})$;
there is a zero vector $\mathbf{0}\in V$ with $\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{v}$;
each $\mathbf{v}$ has an additive inverse $-\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v}+(-\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$;
$a(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=a\mathbf{u}+a\mathbf{v}$;
$(a+b)\mathbf{v}=a\mathbf{v}+b\mathbf{v}$;
$(ab)\mathbf{v}=a(b\mathbf{v})$;
$1\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$.
Elements of $V$ are called vectors. If the scalars come from $\C$ instead of $\R$ we speak of a complex vector space; the theory is identical until Chapter 11.
These are exactly the eight rules of Theorem 1.3 for $\R^n$. Some immediate consequences, which follow from the axioms alone, are worth proving once.

In every vector space: (i) $\mathbf{0}$ is unique and each $-\mathbf{v}$ is unique; (ii) $0\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ and $a\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$; (iii) $(-1)\mathbf{v}=-\mathbf{v}$; (iv) if $a\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ then $a=0$ or $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$.

(ii) $0\mathbf{v}=(0+0)\mathbf{v}=0\mathbf{v}+0\mathbf{v}$; add $-(0\mathbf{v})$ to both sides to get $\mathbf{0}=0\mathbf{v}$. Similarly $a\mathbf{0}=a(\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0})=a\mathbf{0}+a\mathbf{0}$. (iii) $\mathbf{v}+(-1)\mathbf{v}=(1+(-1))\mathbf{v}=0\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$, so $(-1)\mathbf{v}$ is an additive inverse, and inverses are unique: if $\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}'$ both invert $\mathbf{v}$ then $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}+(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}')=(\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{w}'=\mathbf{w}'$. Uniqueness of $\mathbf{0}$ is similar. (iv) If $a\ne0$, multiply $a\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ by $a^{-1}$ to get $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$.
$\R^n$ and $\C^n$ with componentwise operations.
$\R^{m\times n}$, the space of $m\times n$ matrices, with entrywise addition and scaling.
$\mathcal{P}_n$, the polynomials of degree at most $n$, and $\mathcal{P}$, all polynomials. (Degree exactly $n$ does not give a vector space: the sum of $t^2$ and $-t^2+t$ has degree $1$.)
$C[a,b]$, the continuous real functions on $[a,b]$, with $(f+g)(t)=f(t)+g(t)$ and $(cf)(t)=cf(t)$.
The set $\R^\infty$ of real sequences $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$, with termwise operations.
The solutions of a homogeneous linear differential equation such as $y''+y=0$; this space is spanned by $\cos t$ and $\sin t$.
The trivial space $\{\mathbf{0}\}$.

The set of vectors in $\R^2$ with both components nonnegative is not a vector space: the additive inverse of $(1,1)$ is not in it. The set $\{(x,y):x+y=1\}$ is not a vector space: it does not contain $\mathbf{0}$. The set $\{(x,y):xy=0\}$ (the two axes) is closed under scaling but not under addition: $(1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1)$ is outside.

Do not memorise the axioms as a list to check; internalise one principle: a vector space is a set where linear combinations make sense. Any collection of objects that can be added and rescaled, with the sensible rules, is a vector space, and every theorem proved from the axioms applies to it.
A subset $W$ of a vector space $V$ is a subspace if $W$ is itself a vector space under the operations of $V$.
Verifying eight axioms each time would be tedious, but most hold automatically because they hold in $V$.
A subset $W\subseteq V$ is a subspace if and only if
$\mathbf{0}\in W$;
$\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in W\Rightarrow\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in W$ (closed under addition);
$\mathbf{v}\in W,\ c\in\R\Rightarrow c\mathbf{v}\in W$ (closed under scaling).
Equivalently, $W$ is nonempty and closed under linear combinations.

A subspace has these properties by definition. Conversely, (S2) and (S3) show that the operations restrict to $W$; axioms (V1), (V2), (V5)–(V8) hold in $W$ because they hold in $V$; (V3) is (S1); and (V4) holds because $-\mathbf{v}=(-1)\mathbf{v}\in W$ by (S3) and Proposition 6.2.

In $\R^3$ the following are subspaces: $\{\mathbf{0}\}$; any line through the origin; any plane through the origin, for instance $\{x+2y-z=0\}$; and $\R^3$ itself. These are all the subspaces of $\R^3$, as Chapter 7 will prove. A line or plane not through the origin is not a subspace.

Inside $\R^{n\times n}$ the symmetric matrices form a subspace (closed under sums and scalars), as do the diagonal, upper triangular and trace-zero matrices. The invertible matrices do not: $I$ and $-I$ are invertible but $I+(-I)=0$ is not. Inside $C[0,1]$, the functions with $f(0)=0$ form a subspace but those with $f(0)=1$ do not.
Combining subspaces

If $U,W$ are subspaces of $V$ then $U\cap W$ is a subspace, and so is the sum $U+W=\{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}:\mathbf{u}\in U,\mathbf{w}\in W\}$. The union $U\cup W$ is a subspace only when one of $U,W$ contains the other.

Both closure properties pass to the intersection. For the sum, $(\mathbf{u}_1+\mathbf{w}_1)+(\mathbf{u}_2+\mathbf{w}_2)=(\mathbf{u}_1+\mathbf{u}_2)+(\mathbf{w}_1+\mathbf{w}_2)\in U+W$ and similarly for scaling. If neither of $U,W$ contained the other, pick $\mathbf{u}\in U\setminus W$ and $\mathbf{w}\in W\setminus U$: then $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}$ is in neither, since $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\in U$ would give $\mathbf{w}\in U$.
The sum $U+W$ is direct, written $U\oplus W$, if $U\cap W=\{\mathbf{0}\}$. Equivalently every vector of $U+W$ has a unique expression $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}$.

For the equivalence: if $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}'+\mathbf{w}'$ then $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}'=\mathbf{w}'-\mathbf{w}\in U\cap W$, so uniqueness holds iff this intersection is trivial. Orthogonal decompositions $\R^n=W\oplus W^\perp$ (Chapter 11) are the most important direct sums.

For any vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k\in V$, the set $\Span\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k\}$ is a subspace, and it is the smallest subspace containing them: every subspace containing all $\mathbf{v}_i$ contains the span.

A sum of two linear combinations, or a scalar multiple of one, is again a linear combination, so the span is a subspace; it contains $\mathbf{0}$ (take all coefficients zero). Any subspace containing the $\mathbf{v}_i$ is closed under linear combinations, hence contains all of them.
Two subspaces attached to every matrix are the central objects of linear algebra.
For $A\in\R^{m\times n}$ with columns $\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_n$:
the column space $\Col A=\Span\{\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_n\}=\{A\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{x}\in\R^n\}\subseteq\R^m$;
the nullspace (kernel) $\Null A=\{\mathbf{x}\in\R^n:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\}\subseteq\R^n$.

The column space is a subspace by Theorem 6.11. For the nullspace: $A\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$, and if $A\mathbf{x}=A\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ then $A(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{0}$. By Chapter 2, then:
$A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is solvable iff $\mathbf{b}\in\Col A$ (the existence question);
the solution is unique iff $\Null A=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ (the uniqueness question);
the full solution set is $\mathbf{x}_p+\Null A$, a translate of the nullspace (Theorem 2.12).

For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0&1\\0&0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$ (already in RREF), the pivot columns are $1$ and $3$. The columns span $\R^2$, so $\Col A=\R^2$. Solving $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ with free variables $x_2=s$, $x_4=t$: $x_1=-2s-t$, $x_3=-t$, so
\Null A=\Span\left\{\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\right\}.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: row operations change the column space

blocks.x: Row operations preserve the nullspace (Theorem 2.5) but not the column space: swapping rows changes the vectors $A\mathbf{x}$. What they preserve is which columns are pivot columns, and therefore the linear relations among the columns. To describe $\Col A$, take the pivot columns of the original matrix $A$, not of its echelon form. Chapter 8 develops this.

A standard check: to show a set is not a subspace, find a failing axiom, usually that it misses $\mathbf{0}$, or two members whose sum or scalar multiple leaves the set. To show it is one, express it as a nullspace $\{\mathbf{x}:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\}$ or a span; both are automatically subspaces. Sets defined by homogeneous linear conditions are subspaces; conditions like $x^2+y^2=1$, $xy=0$, $x\ge0$ or $x+y=1$ never are.

sections.title: Linear maps and the idea of structure

blocks.x: The best way to compare vector spaces is by functions that respect the structure; this is developed in Chapter 9. For now we record the definition, since it explains why column space and nullspace are the natural subspaces.

A function $T:V\to W$ between vector spaces is linear if $T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=T\mathbf{u}+T\mathbf{v}$ and $T(c\mathbf{v})=cT\mathbf{v}$. Its kernel is $\ker T=\{\mathbf{v}:T\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\}$ and its image is $\im T=\{T\mathbf{v}:\mathbf{v}\in V\}$.
The map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ has kernel $\Null A$ and image $\Col A$, and both are always subspaces.
A vector space is any set with addition and scalar multiplication obeying eight axioms; $\R^n$, matrices, polynomials, functions, sequences and solution spaces of linear equations are examples.
A subset is a subspace iff it contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition and scaling.
Intersections and sums of subspaces are subspaces; unions generally are not. A sum is direct when the intersection is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$.
The span of vectors is the smallest subspace containing them.
Every matrix has a column space (where $A\mathbf{x}$ lives) and a nullspace (the solutions of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$); existence and uniqueness of solutions are statements about them.
Show that the set of $n\times n$ matrices with trace zero is a subspace of $\R^{n\times n}$, and that the set of matrices with determinant $1$ is not.
Prove that if $U$ and $W$ are subspaces of $V$ with $U\cup W$ a subspace, then $U\subseteq W$ or $W\subseteq U$.
Show that every function $f:\R\to\R$ is uniquely a sum $f=f_e+f_o$ of an even and an odd function, and conclude $\{\text{functions}\}=\{\text{even}\}\oplus\{\text{odd}\}$.
Find a spanning set of $\Null A$ and of $\Col A$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\2&2&4\\1&2&3\end{pmatrix}$.
In $\R^{2\times2}$ let $S$ be the symmetric and $K$ the skew-symmetric matrices. Show $\R^{2\times2}=S\oplus K$.
Let $V$ be the set of positive reals with the operations $x\oplus y=xy$ and $c\odot x=x^c$. Verify that $V$ is a vector space. What is its zero vector?
Prove that the set of solutions of $y''-3y'+2y=0$ is a vector space, and that $e^t$ and $e^{2t}$ lie in it. (We will see in Chapter 7 that these two functions span it.)
